https://business-review.eu/bucharest-goi.text: Haferland Week 2026 returns to ten Transylvanian Saxon villages this week The 14th edition of Haferland Week will bring around 60 cultural events to ten villages in Transylvania’s historic “Oat Country”, with fortified church tours, concerts, traditional dances, craft workshops and activities dedicated to the Saxon diaspora. Organisers expect more than 8,000 visitors from Romania and abroad. Haferland Week, one of Romania’s largest festivals dedicated to Transylvanian Saxon heritage, will return between August 6 and 9, 2026, with events taking place across Archita, Saschiz, Homorod, Rupea, Criț, Roadeș, Meșendorf, Cloașterf, Bunești and Viscri. The four-day programme will include approximately 60 activities for visitors of all ages. These range from guided tours of fortified churches and historic sites to concerts, theatre performances, traditional dance, conferences and craft workshops for children and adults. Several of the churches included in the festival route are part of UNESCO-listed heritage sites. Admission to all activities will be free, with no age restrictions. The 2026 edition will be held under the patronage of Romanian Senate President Mircea Abrudean and former Olympic gymnast Nadia Comăneci. This year marks five decades since Comăneci received the first perfect score of 10 in Olympic gymnastics history at the 1976 Montreal Games. Read more about Rediscovering Romania through tourism, design, and heritage read more Jazz, Saxon music and the traditional ball in Criț Music will remain central to the programme. Luiza Zan and Jazzpar Trio will perform a recital dedicated to Maria Tănase in Cloașterf, while Rupea Fortress will host a jazz concert featuring Zan, Mariano Castro and Muse Quartet. Criț will once again host the traditional Saxon ball, accompanied by Nürnberg-based band Flamingo Sound. The village will also be the setting for a brass band parade on Saturday afternoon, bringing together Kulturwerk der Siebenbürger Sachsen, Original Karpaten-Express and Siebenbürger Trachtenkapelle Göppingen. A separate event in the courtyard of the fortified church will mark five years of collaboration between Haferland Week and Kulturwerk der Siebenbürger Sachsen. The organisers estimate that the festival will attract more than 8,000 visitors, including members of the Transylvanian Saxon diaspora returning to the villages connected to their families. Kira Hagi explores memory and the idea of home The festival will host AGAPI – Half a Century of Love , an exhibition by artist and actress Kira Hagi. Designed as an immersive space combining images, objects and sound, the installation examines the idea of home as a place of memory, continuity and personal attachment. The project draws on the meaning of the Greek word meraki , also used in the Aromanian dialect, which describes doing something with care, devotion and personal commitment. Visitors will be invited to consider their own roots and their relationship with the places they define as home. The theme of returning to one’s origins was also reflected during the press conference announcing the 2026 edition. Michael Schmidt donated a traditional dowry chest from Criț, dated 1897, to the Dimitrie Gusti National Village Museum in Bucharest. Previously held in the Michael Schmidt Foundation collection, the object will now become part of the museum’s holdings and will be available to the wider public. The donation recognises the museum’s long-standing support for the festival and extends the foundation’s work to preserve the material heritage of the Transylvanian Saxon communities. Youth Haferland welcomes international participants The third edition of Youth Haferland will run alongside the main programme in partnership with The Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award Romania. The educational and adventure camp connects young participants with local communities, cultural heritage and civic activities. In 2026, the initiative will welcome international teams from Bulgaria and the Czech Republic for the first time, alongside the Romanian team. The Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award provides a structured programme of non-formal education for young people aged between 14 and 24. Globally, it operates under the patronage of the Duke of Edinburgh, while its Romanian programme is held under the patronage of Margareta, Custodian of the Romanian Crown. A festival connecting heritage and the Saxon diaspora Haferland Week was founded 14 years ago by Michael Schmidt and Romanian-born German musician Peter Maffay as a joint project dedicated to recovering, preserving and strengthening the cultural memory of the Transylvanian Saxons. The name Haferland, or “Oat Country”, refers to the area between Rupea and Sighișoara, where the cooler climate historically favoured the cultivation of oats. Today, the region is known for its fortified churches, traditional houses, rural landscapes and the heritage of Saxon communities whose members now live across Romania, Germany and other parts of Europe. The festival is organised by the Michael Schmidt Foundation and the Tabaluga Foundation/Peter Maffay Stiftung, in partnership with the Dimitrie Gusti National Village Museum. The programme is supported by local authorities, heritage organisations, Saxon cultural associations and community groups active across the participating villages. https://thefrontierpost.com/putin-repeat.text: For Western leaders, the Kremlin’s plans to raise defence spending even further, financed with massive new tax increases, will merely confirm their fears about Vladimir Putin’s ultimate aim of provoking a broader conflict with the Nato alliance. After Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte issued his wake-up call last year that Russia could mount an attack against the alliance within five years, there have been numerous warnings that some form of Russian aggression could take place even earlier. Only last week Polish foreign minister Radoslaw Sikorski told a meeting at the UN General Assembly that Moscow is “cooking up something big this year”, while some European intelligence chiefs are warning that Russia could attempt to test Nato’s defences within “months, not years”. Mounting concerns over Putin’s intentions towards Nato are said to explain the decision by CIA director John Ratcliffe to fly to Moscow in late August to warn Putin of the risks he faced if he did provoke a confrontation with the Western alliance. Reports that Moscow is planning to raise military spending in 2027 by a whopping 27 per cent will merely confirm the view that, despite the numerous setbacks Putin has suffered during the Ukraine conflict, the Russian leader has lost none of his appetite for provoking a wider European war. But Putin’s aggression is also coming with an increasingly high cost for Russia itself. Increasing defence spending to £154bn next year – more than twice the size of the UK defence budget, and well over 7 per cent of GDP – will only increase the hardship of ordinary Russians, for whom the personal cost of the Ukraine conflict is becoming abundantly clear. The increase means that around 35 per cent of the Kremlin’s total budget will be spent on a conflict that was only supposed to last a few weeks at most when Putin first launched his “special military operation” against Ukraine in February 2022. Since then his forces are estimated to have suffered 1.5 million casualties, including 500,000 fatalities, as his military campaign has effectively ended in stalemate. The conflict’s impact on the Russian economy has been equally dire, with household incomes falling and public spending on essential services, such as health and education, being drastically cut. Some Russian regions have cut health costs by more than a third during this year alone. Nor is there much prospect of any revival in Russia’s economic fortunes as Western sanctions continue to impact Moscow’s ability to maintain oil and gas exports at pre-war levels. Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure are having similarly deleterious effects. Swathes of Russia suffered fuel shortages over the summer. Putin’s decision, therefore, to divert even more of the country’s resources into fuelling the Kremlin’s war machine should be seen as a desperate gamble, one that could ultimately lead to the collapse of his despotic regime. The Russian regime’s plan to raise the budget allocation for defence to levels not seen since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 should certainly serve as a sobering reminder of the potential pitfalls Putin faces if his gamble does not pay off. Soaring Soviet expenditure on defence from Brezhnev in the 1960s onwards, compounded by Moscow’s disastrous military intervention in Afghanistan from 1979-1989, was one of the key factors that ultimately resulted in the Soviet bloc’s eventual disintegration. On top of the massive economic distortions it resulted in, including shortages of consumer goods, it resulted in powerful vested interests and huge inefficiencies in the military-industrial complex. The Ukraine conflict is proving just as costly for the Kremlin as the Soviets’ Afghan misadventure. It was a point, moreover, that Ratcliffe was keen to stress to Russian officials during the CIA director’s surprise visit to the Kremlin. Apart from bluntly telling his Russian hosts that “Russia is losing the war” in Ukraine, he was at pains to remind them that the current parlous state of the Russian economy showed all the signs that the country faced the risk of a Soviet-style collapse. A subsequent CIA report of the meeting circulated to Western intelligence agencies said that Ratcliffe had concluded the Russian economy “will collapse, just as it did in the Soviet Union at the end of the Cold War”. The ongoing impact of US sanctions on Russia would be a significant contributing factor to this process. Seen in the context of Ratcliffe’s warning, Putin’s decision to divert precious resources to increasing the defence budget seems perverse, especially as the announcement comes after his special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, met with US officials earlier this week for talks on ending the Ukraine war. If Putin is really serious about ending the war, then why increase defence spending? It could be that, despite the inherent weakness of his position, Putin is still trying to send a message to the Trump administration that he has no intention of backing down unless his peace terms are met in Ukraine. But, by repeating the same mistakes the Soviet Union made in raising defence expenditure to unsustainable levels, the Russian leader could ultimately find himself facing the same fate as his Soviet forebears. https://www.politico.eu/article/former-f.text: Philipp Lahm, the former international defender who captained Germany to victory at the 2014 World Cup, has been tapped by his country's government to tackle another challenge: helping young Germans find the best savings account. Lahm will become a "financial education ambassador" alongside actress Tomomi Themann, the ministry announced Wednesday. Both will work pro bono. “As an ambassador for financial education, I want to highlight its value in making informed choices about how we live our lives, and do my part to make it accessible to society at large,” the ministry quoted him as saying in a press release . Advertisement Advertisement Lahm's new job description calls for him to act as a “bridge-builder,” reaching people online, in clubs and at schools to “explain financial topics in an accessible way and to encourage people to take an active interest in their financial future.” The move is part of a new government strategy to strengthen financial literacy in Germany, particularly among young people and women. Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is pitching the strategy as a way to promote greater equality. “Financial education is a matter of fairness. Only with the necessary financial knowledge does everyone have the chance to build an independent life and decide their own future,” the minister said in the press release. Klingbeil is set to meet with Lahm and students at a Berlin school on Friday.

Review The Journalists Who Left Russia—But Can’t Escape It An intimate documentary follows a group of exiles determined to tell their country the truth. November 13, 2026, 2:56 PM By Anastasia Edel , a writer and social historian. And what if that country is Russia? Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile. What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia? Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile. Loktev’s protagonists, almost all women, fled as Russia imposed censorship laws that made their already dangerous jobs punishable by up to 15 years in prison . Within days of Dozhd’s disbandment, sometimes hours, they scooped up their laptops, pets, children, and underwear and flew wherever they could without a new visa—Istanbul, Tbilisi, Prague, Tel Aviv. They resisted Russian President Vladimir Putin and his government, yet wherever they go, they remain citizens of a country that is invading and killing its neighbors and are held responsible for the war it wages in their name. “You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew” says journalist Anna Nemzer, as she reloads her vape cartridge. Loktev’s subjects are buffeted by cognitive dissonance and must constantly explain themselves—to their Georgian and Latvian hosts, who urge them to “tell Putin to stop the war”; to their Ukrainian sources, who resent the very language that they speak; to their Russian parents who tell them to stop writing anti-government “bullshit” and come home; and even to themselves, wondering what they could have done differently to stop their country’s slide into fascism, and whether their work matters when Russian missiles continue to rain down on Ukraine. Loktev, who shot the film herself on an iPhone, gives these questions room. At six hours, this film is even longer than its predecessor—a bold choice—but the sheer accumulation of ordinary moments makes this exploration of exile intimate and compelling. For viewers willing to grapple with existential dilemmas and lucky enough to live near an art-house cinema, the movie’s length may be a boon. After all, its central questions are ones that take a lifetime to sort out. Perhaps no one takes up these questions more bluntly than Elena Kostyuchenko of the recently shuttered Novaya Gazeta , where, during her tenure, four of her colleagues were murdered. “All of us … spent many years, thoroughly, in great detail, in very good, well-written articles describing the coming of fascism in Russia,” she says. “Well, there you fucking go. So we wrote all those articles.” Elsewhere, she is just as unsparing about the failure to stop Putin from turning Russia into what it is today: “We didn’t want to sacrifice our comfort.” Alesya Marokhovskaya expresses similar unease as she recalls watching someone get beaten at a protest. “My job is to film,” she says. “You don’t rush in to defend the person. You film them, because, well, that’s your job.” Despite those doubts, the journalists keep doing journalism. They provide truthful coverage of the war to Russian-speaking audiences through YouTube channels, podcasts, and eventually live broadcasts from Riga, Latvia, where Dozhd secured a broadcasting license. But they are walking on eggshells. A series of on-air missteps that led to questions about the station’s allegiances ultimately cost Dozhd its initial broadcasting license, forcing it to relocate to the Netherlands, where it operates today. A close-up of a woman in a black shirt holding a red pen near her mouth while looking down at a glowing smartphone screen. Irina Dolinina continues to work in exile from Prague. Cinetic The hope of finding safety outside Russia does not last long. Alesya and her best friend Irina Dolinina, investigative journalists with IStories (or Important Stories), now based in Prague, receive oddly specific anonymous threats. The senders know their passport numbers, flight reservations, even about Alesya’s “snorting” bulldog. New friends are not always who they say they are: A supposed human rights lawyer Irina befriends previously worked for Moscow police. Alesya’s father, meanwhile, doesn’t understand why his daughter left. The war is in Ukraine, he says, not Russia. But for most of these women, war is everywhere. From a temporary shelter in a Swiss village, where cathedral bells mark the hours of another peaceful day, Kostyuchenko recounts the symptoms of what she believes was a deliberate poisoning in Munich in October 2022: foul sweat, disorientation, nausea, swollen extremities. Months before, reporting from the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, Kostyuchenko had visited a morgue overflowing with victims of Russian shelling, which she wrote about with brutal clarity. “In the fridge, the bodies are stacked in layers. Two girls lie on top of each other. They’re sisters. The older one is 17—in the heap of bodies, all I can see is her hand, long thin fingers with a neat pink manicure. The younger is 3—she lies on top of her sister. … Her body is dotted with red shrapnel wounds. The girl looks alive.” Despite atrocities that should have stopped the world in its tracks, life goes on, and Loktev’s film captures that well. Kostyuchenko loves, and loves deeply. Her partner is Yana Kuchina, a Moscow book editor turned disability-rights advocate who followed Kostyuchenko into exile. A newcomer to Loktev’s saga, Yana delivers some of the film’s most chilling insights into how Russia treats its own. Her cerebral palsy, she says, is considered an “intellectual inadequacy” in the eyes of the authorities, barring her from getting a driver’s license, becoming a doctor, or adopting a child. Ksenia Mironova and co-director Julia Loktev speak after a screening of My Undesirable Friends: Part II: Exile at the New York Film Festival on Sept. 27. Michael Loccisano/Getty Images Besides Yana, Kostyuchenko loves her mother—whose birthday she is missing for the first time—and her country. Her life there, she felt, was real. “I worked at the best newspaper on Earth. … All around me was my country, which I … value and love still.” Her love is definitely not blind, but for Ukrainians, whose country Russia is destroying, it may be difficult to comprehend, much less forgive. Unlike Elena and Yana, former Dozhd reporter Ksenia (Ksyusha) Mironova walks the road of exile alone, a melancholy kaleidoscope of taxi rides, dark staircases, and endless rented rooms; her fiancé, the journalist Ivan Safronov, is still being held in a Moscow prison on fabricated charges of high treason. Ksyusha returns to Russia for his sentencing, a trip Loktev also documents. Ivan gets 22 years. In the midst of so much loss, there are brief moments of tenderness. In a rented apartment abroad, Ksyusha and her Dozhd friends sing along to a Russian song: “When you return … I hope we recognize each other … and I am not your wife and not even your girlfriend.” It is probably the most Russian scene in the entire movie—elegiac, haunting, yet oddly hopeful. In a dimly lit room, a woman in a red plaid shirt rests her chin in her hand in the foreground while a man and a woman hug behind her. After leaving Russia with her family, Anna Nemzer spent time in Tblisi, Georgia. Cinetic Ksyusha is neither a victim nor a tragic heroine; behind her soft, girlish looks is a rod of steel. No longer with Dozhd, she moves from country to country, taking whatever freelance jobs she can find to keep herself afloat and working as an independent journalist covering political prisoners, their families, and the lives of Russians in exile . In 2025, we see her in the United States reporting on President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “It’s really strange I’m now in America and the same things are happening here,” she says. She now works with Nemzer to archive independent journalism, including to preserve two decades of coverage in Russia against the Kremlin’s attempts to erase it. Sonya Groysman, another Dozhd journalist, finds ingenious ways to report on Russia from exile, directing anonymous camera operators, including wedding videographers. One of her reports features Sasha Skochilenko, an artist who was sentenced to seven years in prison for replacing price tags in a St. Petersburg supermarket with anti-war messages. The camera zooms in on a black-and-white tag above the coffee cans reading “Russia’s Army bombed Mariupol art school where 400 people hid from shelling.” It’s yet another reminder that in Russia, the price of truth is your freedom. Or your life. A sizable part of the documentary is devoted to the 2024 death of opposition leader Alexey Navalny. Dozhd, broadcasting from Amsterdam, ran videos of him from the day before his death, where he looks energetic and fairly healthy. In their coverage, the presenters called his death in prison what many in Russia knew but were afraid to say: a killing. Navalny went to prison to change people’s minds, says tearful Valeria Ratnikova, a Dozhd news anchor, between the airings of her show. He was a beacon for many. Now, all she sees is “total blackness ahead.” A woman with long brown hair, wearing a dark coat and a red patterned scarf, sits on a bed with a blue tufted headboard in front of patterned beige wallpaper. Valeria Ratnikova stays in a hotel in Istanbul after fleeing Russia. Cinetic The only characters spared this Dostoyevskian moral anguish are, unsurprisingly, Ukrainian. “We don’t have the energy and time to worry and panic,” says Nataliya Gumenyuk, a prominent Ukrainian journalist and war correspondent who is married to a longtime former Dozhd journalist. “We live in our own country and continue to do our work.” Among the movie’s most striking images is that of Ukrainians dancing in a square in Kharkiv, where entire blocks are flattened by air strikes, the sound of Ukrainian folk songs mixing with the howling of the air raid sirens. Nataliya’s Russian husband, Peter, resolved his moral dilemma by joining the Ukrainian army and now records his Fuck the War! podcast between missions. From its new home in the Netherlands, the “optimistic channel,” as Dozhd was once known, still reaches 13 million as of 2023, according to Dozhd. Because coverage of the war not aligning with Kremlin narratives has been all but silenced, most watch through VPNs and proxies. For journalists, reporting on Russia’s war means living the Russian reality. This makes integration into their new countries nearly impossible; they are neither here nor there. But going home is not an option. Ratnikova, for one, was sentenced to seven-and-a-half years in prison in absentia by a Moscow court. Loktev records her hearing over a video call, where “witnesses” explain how the “false information” about the war “confused” them. This is how Russian justice works. For now, Ratnikova has a visa, a job, a place to stay. That could change overnight. Political exile is not war, but that’s a low bar for young men and women who could have lived a relatively normal life. By reporting independently, first in an increasingly authoritarian state, then from exile, often at considerable risk to themselves, they have given more to their country than its perpetually silent majority. One of Ratnikova’s colleagues likens their mission to Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill: not as punishment, but by choice. They keep at it, hoping their work might still change minds in a country that seems irretrievably lost. Loktev’s immersion in their lives leaves us with hope for them, if not for Russia’s future.
